lead: The best-kept secret of Valencian gastronomy. Four ingredients, your hands and patience. The contrast between salted cod and the sweetness of roasted pepper, united by the best olive oil in the terreta.

Esgarraet is the antipode of paella: while paella requires technique, fire, exact proportions and a specific vessel, esgarraet asks only for four good ingredients, your hands and time. It is the dish Valencians prepare from one day to the next and take out of the fridge when visitors arrive, when a quick aperitif is needed or when you simply fancy something cold, tasty and well-rounded.

It is found on the counters of the bars of the Cabanyal and the Malvarrosa, in the kitchens of the villages of La Ribera, on the tables of El Carmen during Holy Week. It is a bar dish, a home dish, a summer dish and a Lent dish. The one invariable rule: plenty of bread to “sucar” the oil at the bottom of the plate. Without that, it is not esgarraet.

items.title: What Esgarraet Is · The Name Explains It All
items.subtitle: Torn by hand · Cod + roasted pepper · Valencia’s best-kept secret
items.body: Esgarraet — from the Valencian for “to tear” — is perhaps the humblest and at the same time most delicious dish in all of Valencian gastronomy. Its name describes its method of preparation perfectly: both the salt cod and the roasted red pepper are torn by hand into thin strips, without knife or scissors, before being mixed with sliced garlic and a generous glug of extra virgin olive oil. The result is a cold salad of intense, balanced flavours: the salty edge of the cod contrasts perfectly with the sweetness of the roasted pepper, and the oil acts as the common thread that ties the whole together. Perfect for whetting the appetite, for accompanying rice dishes or simply for dipping bread — “sucar”, as they say in Valencia — in the oil left on the plate. It is surprising how such a simple preparation can yield something so rich in nuance.
facts: Minimum ingredients: 4 · Preparation time: 20 min · Rest in the fridge: at least 2–5 h · Ideal made a day ahead

items.title: The “English” Cod · The Star Ingredient
items.subtitle: Salt-cured cod · Partially desalted · Compact, golden flesh
items.body: The cod used in esgarraet is the so-called “bacalao inglés” (English cod): a cod cured in salt and partially desalted after the curing process, so that it is ready to eat directly without needing to be desalted beforehand. It has compact flesh and a characteristic golden colour that sets it apart from fresh cod. Its salty edge is the element that gives esgarraet its character: that contrast between the saltiness of the cod and the sweetness of the roasted pepper is the basis of the whole recipe. You can also use shredded cod already flaked, but the most authentic version starts from a piece that is flaked by hand, tearing the flesh into strips following the natural grain of the fish. The better the cod, the better the esgarraet: there are no ingredients to hide behind.
facts: English cod: salt-cured, partially desalted, ready to eat directly · Golden colour · Compact flesh

items.title: The Technique · The Hands Are the Instrument
items.subtitle: No knife · No scissors · Tear the pepper · Flake the cod · Marinate in the fridge
items.body: The preparation of esgarraet has its own ritual. The red pepper is roasted directly over the flame or in the oven until the skin separates from the flesh. It is left to cool, peeled and torn by hand into irregular strips — never cut with a knife, because cutting changes the texture and the marinating. The same goes for the cod: it is flaked with the fingers following the natural grain. Everything is placed in a bowl or wide serving dish, the sliced or chopped garlic is added (without overdoing it) and it is generously drizzled with extra virgin olive oil — plenty, because afterwards you have to “sucar” the bread. It is covered with cling film and left to rest in the fridge. The fundamental trick is patience: the minimum is 2 hours, the ideal is a day ahead. During that rest the oil takes on the flavour of the cod and the pepper, the cod rehydrates, the garlic softens its power and the whole becomes something much more than the sum of its parts.
facts: Peppers: roasted over direct fire or in the oven · Torn with the hands · Rest: at least 2 h, ideally 24 h

items.title: The Sucar · The Oil Is the Silent Protagonist
items.subtitle: Sucar · Dipping the bread · EVOO as the common thread · The final reward
items.body: In Valencian, “sucar” means to dip bread in the oil or sauce of a dish. And in esgarraet, the sucar is not an extra: it is the climax of the experience. The extra virgin olive oil, soaked for hours in the juices of the cod and the roasted pepper, acquires a complexity of flavour impossible to achieve any other way. It is salty, sweet, smoky and rounded all at once. The bottom of the plate — that pool of dark, aromatic oil — is what Valencians enjoy most at the end of the meal. It is always served with plenty of bread. Some also accompany it with black olives or mojama in thin slices. Esgarraet is eaten cold, straight from the fridge, and with the hand if need be. It is the most Mediterranean dish in Valencia.
facts: Sucar = dipping bread, in Valencian · EVOO oil + cod juice + pepper = the best sauce in the world

items.title: Variations · Esgarraet Across the Comunitat
items.subtitle: With black olives · With mojama · With roasted aubergine · With ñora · La Ribera style
items.body: Strictly speaking, authentic esgarraet contains only cod, roasted red pepper, garlic and oil. But the recipe has variations as prized as the original. The presentation with black olives is the most common in the bars of Valencia. The version with thin slices of mojama on top adds a point of concentrated, unmatched marine flavour. In the villages of inland Castellón there is a variation with roasted aubergine, which replaces or is added to the pepper. The La Ribera-style esgarraet uses peppers roasted directly over the flame — not in the oven —, a thicker, well-desalted cod, plenty of oil and a long rest: the result is more intense and powerful. In every case, the essence is the same: the contrast between the salted cod and the sweetness of the pepper, with the oil as the bridge.
facts: Basic version: cod + pepper + garlic + EVOO · Variations: + black olives / + mojama / + roasted aubergine

items.title: Always with the hands
items.body: Never knife or scissors — tearing by hand gives a texture that cutting cannot replicate

items.title: English cod, not fresh
items.body: Salt-curing is essential — the salty edge is the DNA of the dish

items.title: Quality roasted pepper
items.body: Over direct flame or in the oven — if from a jar, make it a good one, because the result shows

items.title: Plenty of EVOO
items.body: Do not skimp: the oil will soak up all the flavour and afterwards you dip bread in it

items.title: Rest at least 2 hours
items.body: Ideally a day ahead — patience is the only trick of this recipe

items.title: Serve well chilled
items.body: Straight from the fridge, with plenty of bread and in no hurry — esgarraet does not wait

blocks.title: What you should know about esgarraet
items: English cod needs no prior desalting — it already comes partially desalted and ready to eat directly
Never use a knife to shred the pepper or the cod — tearing by hand is part of the recipe, not a detail
The olive oil must be plentiful and of good quality — it is the ingredient that transforms the dish during marinating
Holy Week is the most traditional time, but esgarraet is perfect all year round — especially in summer, well chilled
Black olives and mojama are the classic accompaniments — they add depth without stealing the show
Bread, plenty of bread — the “sucar” in the oil at the bottom of the plate is the most Valencian part of the whole experience
